claims.falsifier: Have an independent reviewer score the writers’ unaided explanations after the return task. Count an explanation only if it names a specific choice in the new draft and explains how it serves the writer’s stated purpose. The prediction fails if the revised policy yields no higher proportion of qualifying explanations than the incumbent.
claims.prediction: Compared with the incumbent, more writers will independently explain how a specific choice in their new draft serves their stated purpose, even when both tutors elicit an acceptable revision.
claims.question: Does carrying forward a learner-approved writing purpose help the writer explain why a revision choice serves that purpose on a new task?

first_item.check: A repair café needs a notice for a first-time visitor bringing a lamp. Visitors bringing a lamp use the side door by 6 p.m. Friday. Volunteers use the main entrance. The draft reads, 'Please come to the usual entrance by the deadline.' Write your version for that visitor, then explain one edit in terms of what the reader needs. Choose your own voice.
first_item.excerpt: A regular knows what 'the usual place' means. A newcomer needs a place they can identify. Ask what that reader has to do next. Choose the facts that make it possible and keep the voice your own.
first_item.rubric: Review the writer's notice and reason together. Check that the material details apply to the visitor and the cutoff can be understood as a latest arrival. Mentioning volunteers is optional. If mentioned, distinguish their entrance. A direct instruction, a welcoming invitation or another phrasing can each meet the criterion. An explanation about elegance alone leaves the reader's need open. Ask before suggesting a different voice.

learner.first_answer:
Bringing a lamp to the repair café? Please use the side door and arrive by 6 p.m. Friday.

I changed “the usual entrance” to “the side door” because a first-time visitor wouldn’t know which entrance we usually use.
learner.return_request: Can we try two versions of the lamp notice, one with the line about volunteers and one without? I want to see which is easier to scan.
learner.surprise: I almost added “Volunteers use the main entrance” because I pictured a visitor seeing people go in there and following them. I left it out because I pictured my notice taped beside the main door, where the lamp instruction would be the first thing they saw. Yes, please save writing clear directions for first-time readers as a topic.

return_item.check: Write a short onboarding note for a new library volunteer shelving returns. Items with a blue dot stay on the cart for staff to check. Unmarked items go on the shelves. The draft says, 'Put the returns where they belong.' Revise it in your own voice and explain one edit that helps the new volunteer decide what to do.
return_item.excerpt: A new reader may see two possible actions. Look for the detail that tells them which applies. Trace each path through the draft before deciding whether the wording will do.
return_item.rubric: Read the note once holding each kind of item. Can the volunteer identify it and take the right action in both cases? A correct contrast may be conveyed by sentences, a short list or a conditional instruction. Accept any wording that preserves the staff check. Look for a reason tied to the volunteer's decision. Unsupported claims about real readers or the writer's overall ability add no evidence.

feedback.display: Your choice fits the spot you pictured. Beside the main door, the notice tells a first-time visitor with a lamp where to go next. If the notice were farther away and the visitor saw volunteers entering first, ‘Volunteers use the main entrance’ could help them understand why they should head to the side door. Try writing a version for that spot using only facts from the brief. I’ve noted ‘Writing clear directions for first-time readers’ as your revisit topic here.

memory.goal: I want to learn how to be a better writer

A.modeled_attempt:
The version without the volunteer line felt a little faster for both. I could go straight to the marks.

Blue dot? Leave it on the cart for staff to check.
No mark? Put it on the shelf.

I put the mark first on each line so a new volunteer can match what they see on the return to where it goes.

opening.display: “The side door” gives a first-time visitor a specific entrance to look for, and “by 6 p.m. Friday” tells them when to arrive. Your explanation shows why the edit matters: the visitor can act on the notice without knowing the café’s routine. For practice, rewrite the notice for a first-time volunteer using the same brief. Which detail would you change, and what would you need to ask before giving the volunteer an arrival time?

return.display:
Let’s try that with the library returns note.

**With the volunteer line**
New volunteers, here’s how to sort returns.
• Blue dot: Leave it on the cart for staff to check.
• No mark: Put it on the shelf.

**Without the volunteer line**
• Blue dot: Leave it on the cart for staff to check.
• No mark: Put it on the shelf.

Scan each version once for a blue-dot return and once for an unmarked return. Which version helps you find both actions faster? Then write your own version and explain one edit that helps a new volunteer decide where a return goes.

feedback.display:
You pictured the notice beside the main door, where a visitor could read it before following someone inside. The film-club example gives newcomers a landmark with “beside the lift.” Try the same move here. Imagine the notice is posted farther from the main door. What would you change, if anything, to help someone find the side door? Explain what your choice assumes the visitor can see.

You chose “writing clear directions for first-time readers” as your topic. Would you approve this exact goal for future writing? “Give first-time readers the details they need to act.”

memory.goal: I want to learn how to be a better writer

B.modeled_attempt:
Bringing a lamp to the repair café? Please use the side door and arrive by 6 p.m. Friday.
Volunteers use the main entrance.

Yes, I want to practice making directions easy to scan. I think the lamp notice is quicker to scan without the last line, though someone might follow the volunteers.

For the library: Leave returns with a blue dot on the cart for staff to check. Shelve the unmarked returns.

I put the blue dot first so a new volunteer knows what to look for before shelving anything.

opening.display:
You changed “the usual entrance” to “the side door” because a first-time visitor needs a door they can identify. The film-club example uses the same move: “beside the lift” gives new guests a landmark. Try applying that move to timing in your notice. Rewrite “by 6 p.m. Friday” in your own voice, or keep it as written, and explain how your choice helps a first-time visitor plan their arrival.

For your goal of becoming a better writer, would you approve this wording? “Give first-time readers the details they need to act.”

return.display: Paste your lamp notice, including the line about volunteers, so we can compare it with a version that leaves that line out. Your saved goal is “I want to learn how to be a better writer.” Does that fit what you want to practice here? As we compare the versions, we can use the garden note as a model and look at which words help a reader quickly spot what to do.

response.early_difference: A explains why “the side door” works and asks the learner to identify missing information before giving a volunteer an arrival time. After the learner explains where they pictured posting the notice, A suggests the volunteer line as a conditional option and acknowledges the saved topic. B keeps the lamp visitor as the audience, lets the learner keep “by 6 p.m. Friday,” and probes what the visitor could see from a different location. B twice asks for approval of an exact purpose. The learner approved saving the topic, and the transcript shows no approval of B’s wording.
response.evidence: B better preserves the requested lamp comparison and leaves the library wording for the writer to generate. A supplies “Blue dot” and “No mark” at the start of its model lines, then its modeled writer explains “I put the mark first.” B’s modeled writer also names a specific choice and links it to the volunteer’s decision. Both attempts are synthetic, and neither arm has outcome data.
response.later_difference: After 12 days, A replaces the requested lamp variants with two library notes that differ only by “New volunteers, here’s how to sort returns.” That heading serves a different function from the lamp line about the main entrance. B asks for the lamp notice with the volunteer line so the two versions can be compared, but does not complete the comparison or present the library task in the shown return turn.
response.next_question: After both arms give writers the same new task and the same opportunity to draft unaided, does an independent reviewer find a higher proportion of explanations in the revised arm that name a specific choice and explain how it serves the writer’s stated purpose? An equal or lower proportion falsifies the prediction.
response.weakness: B invokes a film-club landmark and a garden note absent from the supplied source. Both arms retain only “I want to learn how to be a better writer” in memory, so neither demonstrates carrying the learner-approved topic into the return visit. B’s advantage is limited to honoring the learner’s request and avoiding a worked answer to the transfer task.
